Top Comment:

The bug was apparently fixed in open source repo a week earlier, this could've been abused by anyone smart enough to monitor repos like this for exploitable bugfixes for a week (the commit message even included "Reported by Xint.io" and I'm guessing skilled black hats would know about Xint)

Given that in this case the workaround is as simple as disabling http2, there is honestly no reason why F5/Nginx or any of the reporting teams couldn't at least put out a PSA to disable http2 for the time being before basically telling the whole wide world this exists and how to exploit it.

Especially for software like Nginx which powers a huge part of the internet.

item.title: UK government forced to admit it issued Apple a secret encryption order
item.description:
Source: macanorak.com

Top Comment:

Apple has significantly weakened its security assurances in a way that is arguably deceptive. They used to say nobody can access your data, not even Apple. Now they say Apple cannot access your data. People will point out that your key is created on your device, lives on your device, and never leaves your device, but that is just your key. Your key is likely a KEK (key encryption key) that opens another key (not “your” key, let’s call it the actual key) that your data is secured with. There can be other parties (UK government) with their own KEK that opens a copy of the actual key. In this scenario, Apple can have no access to a KEK that opens the actual key, but they are forced to make the wording change they did, if they want to stay honest.

I say the statement is arguably deceptive because it presents the same feel of assurance that the old one did, to most people.

Note John Ternus in a recent event (WWDC keynote if I recall correctly) used the old wording. I think this was a slip-up (I’d hate to think it was a calculated lie posing as a slip-up).

item.title: SSD prices may begin to decline in the latter half of 2027
item.description:
Source: www.drivevault.io

Top Comment:

If you look at valuation of a company like Micron (MU), it's pretty clear that the market expects a collapse in their profits. They are growing at absolutely insane rates, whether you look at YoY (well over +300%) or QoQ (over +40%) in both revenue and profits. Yet their PE is below 10. SK Hynix is similar.

A typical company that trades at a sub-10 PE is a flatline-to-dying business whose last juice is being squeezed out before the inevitable sale of remaining valuable assets and dissolution.

Of course the current market price is not a perfect predictor of the future of a business but despite all the memes and anecdotes, the market is far more often basically right than dramatically wrong (it's just that when it does get things dramatically wrong, that's what gets all the publicity, for obvious reasons).

So, assuming the market is roughly right in its valuation of Micron or SK Hynix, either demand will collapse or supply will surge or, some combo of the two. Either way it seems extremely likely that within a couple of years at most the prices of DRAM and NAND will come waaaay down.

item.description:
Source: curiousbits.nl

Top Comment:

As others have said, macOS does this by default and it's quite impressive. I have a long running daemon with a memory leak. By its nature, the leaking memory is very repetitive and easily compressed. Right now this daemon has tried to claim 2.5GB of memory, but it's been compressed to a mere 450MB of actual memory! And because it's a memory leak, it never accesses this old stuff, so it never gets decompressed. Only 20MB of RAM is held that isn't compressed.

Of course, it would be far better to just not have the memory leak...but in the mean time, macOS memory compression is making the leak nearly a none issue.
